text.p: The Australian Cricket Board (ACB) on Tuesday changed its tune about crowd entertainment at one-day matches amid fears their innovative musical approach might offend opposition batsmen.
ACB officials said they would stop playing certain songs to celebrate the fall of an opposition wicket in case the players and spectators find the lyrics unsporting.
Departing West Indies batsmen heard such songs as "Hit the Road, Jack", "Return to Sender" or "See You Later, Alligator" as they walked to the pavilion during recent matches against Australia.
In contrast, there was no music broadcast over the public address system to accompany the Australia batsmen as they trudged off the field during the World Series games on Friday and Sunday.
The use of the soundtrack prompted a critical editorial in Melbourne's The Age newspaper on Tuesday.

"There used to be....polite applause as batsmen began their long walk back to the pavilion. Now there are bursts of amplified pop music, apparently selected with intimidation or humiliation in mind," The Age said.
ACB marketing manager David Fouvy said certain songs would be dropped so that the emphasis could be placed on positive aspects of the game rather than stressing a player's misfortune.
"We found that it was not appropriate because there was a risk these songs could be misunderstood," Fouvy told Reuters.
"We did not want there to be any chance that the songs might be seen as gloating," he said. "Our intention is to focus on great batting, bowling and fielding."
He said other songs, such as Queen's "We Will Rock You", will still be used as well as sound effects, including the voice of cartoon character Homer Simpson.
Several dozen spectators were ejected for misbehaving during the limited overs matches in Sydney and Melbourne, while several people ran onto the pitch during play.

"What the (ACB) should consider is the danger that our one-day cricket matches will slide from being exciting expositions of national sporting pride and individual prowess to tacky little sideshows of hoons (hooligans) and hype," The Age commented.
